sections.h2: Where do McLean County property owners take tax questions?
sections.html:
Valuation questions go to the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA), and payment questions go to the Sheriff. McLean County's PVA takes mail at P.O. Box 246, Calhoun, KY 42327, and can be reached at (270) 273-3291. The Sheriff's Office is at 135 East 2nd Street in Calhoun, and the county Sheriff page links to an online property tax records lookup for checking an account.

Keep the two roles apart. The PVA assigns the assessment as of January 1 and processes exemptions. It cannot accept money. The Sheriff takes payments through April 15 and hands whatever is left to the County Clerk. If you are buying or selling in Calhoun, Livermore, Island or Sacramento, the same two offices serve every address in the county.

sections.h2: What does it cost to pay a McLean County bill late?
sections.html:
The price of waiting is fixed by KRS 134.015 and climbs each month the bill is open. A 2 percent discount applies if the full amount reaches the Sheriff by November 1, and in 2026 that date has already passed. The rest of the sequence looks like this:

  • November 2 to December 31: pay the bill as printed.
  • January 1 to 31: a 5 percent penalty.
  • From February 1: a 10 percent penalty.
  • April 15: the Sheriff stops collecting and sends open bills to the County Clerk.

Should bills be mailed late, the Department of Revenue can move to an alternative schedule that gives owners one month for the discount, one month at face value and one month at the 5 percent penalty. Either way, the unpaid balance is the taxpayer's personal debt from the assessment date.

sections.h2: How large is a typical McLean County tax bill?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau puts the median home value at $148,500, and the state's 2025 rate of 10.6 cents per $100 turns that into about $157.41 of state tax. Rates set by the fiscal court, the school district and other taxing bodies are layered on, so the PVA is the place to ask for an address-specific total.

sections.h2: Does McLean County offer a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Yes, under the same state rule as every Kentucky county. Owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, can have $49,100 removed from the assessed value for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. Roughly 22.5 percent of McLean County residents are 65 or older, so many households could qualify.

On a $148,500 home the taxable amount becomes $99,400, and the state's slice falls to about $105.36. Apply at the PVA, and bring a driver's license, birth certificate or passport to prove age. Disability applicants must show total disability under a federal or retirement-system program and, in most cases, renew yearly. Exceptions are veterans with a service-connected disability and people already ruled totally and permanently disabled by Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement Systems. If you sell, tell the PVA so the exemption is not left on the old address.

sections.h2: How can a McLean County owner appeal a value?
sections.html:
An owner has to meet with the PVA before filing anything. The conference is the step that opens the door to the board of assessment appeals.

  • The roll is open for inspection for 13 days, starting the first Monday in May, and notice of the dates runs in the largest local newspaper.
  • At the conference the PVA must explain the basis of your assessment, and a record form is kept.
  • The appeal itself is filed with the County Clerk by close of business the day after inspection ends.
  • Evidence is required: building and land descriptions, insurance records, construction costs and sale listings. Without it, the board denies the appeal.

The board meets 25 to 35 days after the inspection period and must explain in writing any change it makes. A paid representative has to be one of the professional types the state lists and show written authority. Missing the hearing forfeits the later appeal to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

sections.h2: What happens if McLean County taxes are unpaid at closing?
sections.html:
The lien stays with the parcel. After the April 15 transfer, the County Clerk holds the bill as a certificate of delinquency, records a lien, and adds interest at 1 percent per month. The lien can last 11 years under KRS 134.420 no matter who owns the house.

Certain costs stack up in order: a 10 percent clerk commission, a 20 percent county attorney commission once notices go out, postage, advertising, and lien recording fees. The Department of Revenue's worked examples show a $1,000 bill reaching a $1,254 certificate before any of those are added. Contact the Sheriff before April 15 for a payoff, and the Clerk after it. A sale of the certificate can be set 90 to 135 days after transfer, and an investor who buys it may add charges of its own.

sections.h2: What should a McLean County seller know about the area?
sections.html:
McLean County was formed on February 6, 1854, from parts of Daviess, Ohio and Muhlenberg counties. It covers 256 square miles in the Western Coal Fields region and sits within the Owensboro metropolitan area. The Green River crosses it from southeast to northwest, with bridge crossings at Calhoun and Livermore, and Army Corps of Engineers Lock and Dam No. 2 at Calhoun helps boats move on the river. The county is dry, meaning alcohol sales are prohibited.

Cities are Calhoun, the seat, Livermore, which is the largest community, Island and Sacramento. A single county-wide school district runs one high school, one middle school and three elementary schools, with elementaries in Calhoun, Livermore and Sacramento. The county keeps Central time, and the Census counted 9,064 residents in 2025, down 1.0 percent from 2020.

The mean commute is 31.4 minutes, and the Census counted only two building permits in 2025. Median household income is $65,596, with 15.8 percent of people below the poverty line. For sellers holding inherited property, a rural parcel, or a house with unpaid tax, a direct cash sale avoids listing and repair costs. Ask the Sheriff for the payoff and the PVA for the parcel record before you set a price.

McLean County borders Henderson, Daviess, Ohio, Muhlenberg, Hopkins and Webster counties. Census figures list 91.7 percent of adults 25 and older as high school graduates, and 85.3 percent of households have a broadband subscription, which helps when you want to look up a bill or download an exemption form. The population peaked at 13,241 in 1910 and has stayed between about 9,000 and 10,100 since 1960.

faqs.q: Does the McLean County PVA accept tax payments?
faqs.a: No. The Sheriff collects payments. The PVA at (270) 273-3291 sets the assessment and takes exemption applications.

faqs.q: When does a McLean County tax bill become delinquent?
faqs.a: The 10 percent penalty starts after January 31, and the Sheriff passes open bills to the County Clerk after April 15. The Clerk adds 1 percent monthly interest and records a lien.

faqs.q: How much is the homestead exemption in McLean County?
faqs.a: It is $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. Owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, apply with the PVA in Calhoun.

faqs.q: What is the state tax on a median McLean County home?
faqs.a: About $157.41 on the $148,500 Census median, using the 2025 state rate of 10.6 cents per $100. County and school rates are extra.

faqs.q: Who hears a McLean County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: A local board of assessment appeals made up of property owners hears it, 25 to 35 days after the inspection period. File with the County Clerk after meeting with the PVA.
